HTSlib is a library for reading and writing bioinformatics file formats. Prior to 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24, the BCF reader can experience an integer overflow in a record-length check that verifies whether a record contains enough bytes for the expected number and size of stored items. A crafted BCF record can bypass this check, causing reads beyond the stored data and, in some cases, writes beyond the heap buffer when the reader sets the least significant bit of accessed bytes. Opening such a file can crash the process, corrupt data or heap structures, and may permit arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in versions 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24.

HTSlib is a library for reading and writing bioinformatics file formats. Prior to 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24, the CRAM decoder validates the 254-character query-name limit only after decoding the name into a 1024-byte stack array. An attacker-controlled CRAM record can provide an overlong query name and overflow the local stack buffer before the later validation runs; all CRAM format versions are affected. Opening such a file can crash the process, corrupt stack data, and may permit arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in versions 1.21.2, 1.22.3, 1.23.2, and 1.24.

modified eCommerce Shopsoftware through 3.3.0 contains a local file inclusion vulnerability that allows administrators to include arbitrary server files by storing ../ sequences in the content manager file name. Unauthenticated requests to shop_content.php then pass the stored path to include(), executing embedded PHP in uploaded content files or images as the web server user.

diaspora* before 0.10.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated users to inject script by crafting og:video:secure_url values. Attackers can post links to pages whose allowlisted-prefix video URL contains a quote and onload handler, executing script in readers' sessions when they click the video preview.

SABnzbd through 5.1.3 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the Sorter that allows attackers to write files outside the Complete folder via crafted propername, episodename or job name (%dn) values. Attackers can supply a malicious NZB with '...' sequences that collapse to '..' after single-pass replacement, moving downloaded files into arbitrary directories writable by SABnzbd.

Stoatchat before 0.16.5 contains an unbounded JXL image decoding vulnerability in revolt_files decode_image that allows unauthenticated attackers to exhaust memory via the january /proxy endpoint. Attackers can request a small hosted JXL file declaring 12000x12000 pixels through /proxy to trigger huge allocations, OOM-killing january and denying proxy and embed service.

Bolt is a fully open source, adaptable platform for building and running modern websites. Prior to 6.1.4, SQL injection in ListFormatHelper allows authenticated users with upload permission to execute arbitrary SQL queries through /async/select-options and exfiltrate sensitive database contents when general/caching/list_format is enabled. This issue is fixed in version 6.1.4.

Daptin is a GraphQL/JSON-API headless CMS. Prior to 0.12.30, the generic GET /api/{entity} list endpoint accepts attacker-controlled sort values in PaginatedFindAllWithoutFilters in server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go without validating the requested column against the table schema. The code uses those values for SELECT and ORDER BY identifier construction, so an embedded identifier quote can terminate the quoted identifier and make the remainder parse as SQL, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to extract unauthorized table data through blind or error-based behavior or repeatedly trigger query failures. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.30.

@scalar/typebox before 0.1.4 contains a code injection vulnerability in TypeCompiler that allows attackers to execute JavaScript by supplying crafted schema strings. Attackers can inject single-quote breakouts into string format, Kind names, property keys or Literal values to run arbitrary JavaScript in the host Node.js process during Compile() and Check().

sqlmap before 1.10.11.89 contains a credential exposure vulnerability that allows attackers to capture user-supplied Cookie and Authorization headers by redirecting requests to another host. Attackers controlling the scanned target or abusing an open redirect can make RedirectHandler.http_error_302 forward session cookies or bearer tokens to an attacker-controlled host.

Sprout Track is a self-hosted baby tracking application. Prior to 1.3.5, Sprout Track uses a publicly known hardcoded signing secret when JWT_SECRET is unset, and standard setup does not generate a unique secret. On a network-reachable affected deployment, an unauthenticated attacker can sign JWTs with arbitrary claims, including system-administrator claims, to access administrative functionality and read or modify family, child activity, account, and email data. Deployments with a strong unique JWT_SECRET are not affected. Managed and hosted instances were reported remediated. This issue is fixed in version 1.3.5.

A flaw was found in GIMP. Opening a crafted XCF with a truncated uncompressed tile can expose uninitialized main-process stack memory through the imported layer's pixel data, which may include process addresses that weaken ASLR.

Git LFS is a Git extension for versioning large files. From 1.3.0 until 3.8.1, Git LFS does not correctly filter the limited set of options permitted in a repository's .lfsconfig file when option keys contain certain additional components. Crafted keys can mimic options that configure Git LFS to use a custom command to transfer objects, causing Git LFS to execute an attacker-selected command or binary while fetching objects. This issue is fixed in version 3.8.1.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. Prior to 3.10.4, Prover9Parent.config_prover9 and Mace accept a relative binary_location and pass it to find_binary as path_to_bin, disabling the bare-name absolute-path guard. A local attacker who can plant prover9 or mace4 in the resolved working directory can cause subprocess.Popen to execute that binary with the invoking user's privileges. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.10.0 until 3.10.4, StreamBackedCorpusView performs os.stat on a caller-supplied plain string path during construction before pathsec containment is enforced. The PathPointer branch used by in-tree corpus readers is validated, so exploitation requires application code to pass an attacker-influenced string directly to the public constructor. That string can identify an out-of-root path and disclose its existence, size, and modification time even though opening the file would be rejected. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. Prior to 3.10.4, DependencyGraph.tree and DependencyGraph.triples walk parsed dependency edges through unbounded Python recursion and do not use a working cycle or depth guard. A crafted CoNLL or Malt-TAB dependency file containing a sufficiently long chain can raise RecursionError when the documented traversal APIs are called, aborting the current worker. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. Prior to 3.10.4, Tree.fromlist recursively converts nested Python list input into Tree objects without enforcing a maximum tree depth. An attacker-controlled list nested beyond the interpreter recursion limit can raise RecursionError and terminate the current parse operation or request worker. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.9.4 until 3.10.4, NLTK corpus-reader path pointers and view methods validate a requested relative path without consistently resolving intermediate directory symlinks against the reader's scoped root. A local attacker who can place such a symlink can make abspaths or words reach a readable file outside the corpus root and disclose its contents. On releases with pathsec enforcement, the file must remain inside a global NLTK allowed root; version 3.9.4 has enforcement disabled and permits a broader escape. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to 7.3.0, the six network address set handlers in cmd/incusd/network_address_sets.go resolved the effective project with project.NetworkProject(), which returns default when features.networks is unset. The expandProject authorization switch in cmd/incusd/daemon.go omitted auth.ObjectTypeNetworkAddressSet, so authorization used the requested project instead of the effective project. This issue is fixed in version 7.3.0.

RepoManager is a self-hosted deb/rpm package repository. Prior to 5.13.3, the authenticated get-unit-log action accepts a caller-controlled logfile value. Validate::string() escapes HTML but leaves path traversal components unchanged. The action joins the caller-controlled logfile to SERVICE_LOGS_DIR without enforcing containment, so traversal can resolve the file read outside that directory. www/controllers/ajax/status/service.php reads and returns the resolved file, and any authenticated user can invoke the action to retrieve files readable by the www-data service account, including application configuration, source code, and the GPG signing-key passphrase. Fixed in 5.13.3.

bep/imagemeta is a Go library for reading EXIF, IPTC and XMP image meta data from JPEG, TIFF, PNG, and WebP files. Prior to 0.17.3, imagemeta.Decode could exhaust memory when parsing PNG zTXt chunks whose keyword is "Raw profile type iptc": the declared chunk length can drive an allocation far larger than the input file, and the embedded zlib stream is decompressed without an output limit. The advisory reports a 42-byte input causing a 256 MB allocation and a 127 KB input inflating to 460 MB. The oversized-allocation path's memory effect depends on platform overcommit and configured GOMEMLIMIT or cgroup limits, while the decompression path reliably creates resident memory. Applications that decode untrusted PNGs with IPTC metadata processing can therefore suffer denial of service through memory exhaustion. This issue is fixed in 0.17.3.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could view credentials configured for email notifications in a saved search shared with that user.
The vulnerability is possible when email notifications use authentication credentials because the Saved Searches Representational State Transfer (REST) API returns those credentials in clear text.
For more information see Search endpoint descriptions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/leverage-rest-apis/rest-api-reference/10.6/search-endpoints/search-endpoint-descriptions), Manage knowledge object permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/manage-knowledge-objects/knowledge-management-manual/10.6/get-started-with-knowledge-objects/manage-knowledge-object-permissions), and Email notification action (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/alert-and-respond/alerting-manual/10.6/configure-alert-actions/email-notification-action) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.0, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who does not hold a role with either the list_indexer_cluster capability or the edit_indexer_cluster capability could download the cluster manager configuration bundle through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API and access configuration and app files that the cluster manager stages for indexer distribution.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API does not require the list_indexer_cluster or edit_indexer_cluster capability before it sends the configuration bundle.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.
For more information see Cluster endpoint descriptions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/leverage-rest-apis/rest-api-reference/10.6/cluster-endpoints/cluster-endpoint-descriptions) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could trick a user who has an active Splunk Web session into selecting the Top values by time field report on the Search page. The selection could run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches and potentially expose stored credentials and indexed data.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Web does not correctly neutralize user-controlled data when it generates an SPL search for a field report.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the user by tricking them into opening a link that the attacker creates. The unauthenticated user should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could craft a shared Classic Dashboard that runs arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands for another authenticated user. Exploitation requires the dashboard viewer to open the shared dashboard. The injected commands could access data available to the dashboard viewer, modify data available to the dashboard viewer, and partially disrupt Splunk Enterprise.
For more information see Add sparklines to search results (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/search/search-manual/10.6/calculate-statistics/add-sparklines-to-search-results), Configure dashboard permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/simple-xml-dashboards/10.6/manage-and-share-dashboards/configure-dashboard-permissions), and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands into a Classic Dashboard search. When another user opens the affected dashboard in Splunk Web, those injected commands execute with the viewing user's permissions, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to access stored credentials and write data to indexes.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape user-supplied content when it rewrites a search, which lets the rewritten search include additional SPL commands.
The vulnerability requires another user to open the dashboard in Splunk Web. Consequently, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, an unauthenticated user could craft a malicious link that, if opened by an authenticated user, executes arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches with the victim's permissions. 
Successful exploitation could allow the unauthenticated user to access or modify data, alter Splunk platform configurations, and disrupt operations available to the affected user.
The vulnerability is possible because the Portable Document Format (PDF) generation component processes request data before it rejects deprecated GET requests and does not apply SPL safeguards for risky commands to subsearches.
For more information see Generate PDFs of your reports and dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/reporting-manual/10.4/report-management/generate-pdfs-of-your-reports-and-dashboards) and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user holding a role with the edit_token_http capability could create a persistent HTTP Event Collector (HEC) token that cannot be disabled or deleted via the Representational State Transfer (REST) API or Splunk Web. As a result, the token remains active and can continue ingesting events even after administrative attempts to revoke it.
The vulnerability is possible because HTTP Event Collector token creation accepts names that later management operations cannot process.
For more information see authorize.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.4/configuration-file-reference/10.4.5-configuration-file-reference/authorize.conf) and Set up and use HTTP Event Collector in Splunk Web (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/get-data-in/get-started-with-getting-data-in/10.6/get-data-with-http-event-collector/set-up-and-use-http-event-collector-in-splunk-web) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the mc_investigation_read capability could cause the Risk Event Timeline Representational State Transfer (REST) API to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands with elevated permissions. With this access, the user could expose stored credentials and modify indexes and lookup data available to those permissions.
The vulnerability is possible because the affected REST API does not validate request values before including them in search macro arguments.
For more information see Capability reference for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/capability-reference-for-splunk-enterprise-security) and Risk analysis (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/risk-analysis) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the mc_investigation_read capability could overwrite Mission Control preference records for other users and remove saved filters and analyst queue settings from those records.
The vulnerability is possible because the Mission Control user preferences Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not bind an update to the preference record that passes the authorization check.
The attack requires the user to obtain a preference record identifier that the product does not normally expose to that user. The user should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Overview of Mission Control in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/mission-control/overview-of-mission-control-in-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the ueba_ers_execution_post capability could cause the User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) Content App to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands with elevated permissions through an Entity Risk Score calculation. With this access, the user could expose stored credentials and other data outside the permissions assigned to that role.
The vulnerability is possible because the UEBA Content App does not validate Entity Risk Score calculation values before including them in SPL searches.
For more information see Installing the UEBA Content App for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.5/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/installing-the-ueba-content-app-for-splunk-enterprise-security), Entity risk scoring in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.4/risk-based-alerting/entity-risk-scoring-in-splunk-enterprise-security), and Roles and knowledge objects in UEBA for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.8/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/ueba-content-app-for-on-premises/roles-and-knowledge-objects-in-ueba-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the edit_timeline capability could store attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) in a legacy investigation timeline entry. Another user that holds a role with the manage_all_investigations capability could later open the investigation and select Run Search from the timeline. Splunk Enterprise Security could then run the SPL stored by the first user using the permissions of the user who selected Run Search. The SPL stored by the first user could access data or perform actions available to the user who selected Run Search.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise Security does not treat stored investigation search content as a literal search before building the Search page link.
For more information see Capability reference for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.3/installation/capability-reference-for-splunk-enterprise-security) and Add details to an investigation in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-7/user-guide/7.3/investigations/add-details-to-an-investigation-in-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in network traffic data. Another user who holds the "pci_user" role could later click the corresponding row in the Traffic Detail panel of the Network Traffic Activity report. Splunk Enterprise Security could then run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who clicked the row. The commands could access data and perform actions available to that user.
The vulnerability is possible because the Network Traffic Activity report does not treat network traffic values as literal search values when it builds the Traffic Detail drilldown search.
For more information see Network Traffic Activity (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-reports/network-traffic-activity) and Configure users and roles (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-the-app/configure-users-and-roles) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in data that populates the Endpoint Changes report. Another user who holds the "pci_analyst" role could later click a corresponding table row. Splunk Enterprise Security could then run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who clicked the row. The commands could access or modify data available to that user.
The vulnerability is possible because the Endpoint Changes report does not treat dynamic report values as literal search values when it builds table-row drilldown searches.
For more information see Reports (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/user-manual/8.7/using-the-splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/reports) and Configure users and roles (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-the-app/configure-users-and-roles) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in vulnerability data. If another user who can access the Vulnerability Search dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Vulnerability Search dashboard encodes data-model field values for the drilldown link but does not escape the values as SPL search literals before inserting the values into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Network dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/network-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, an unauthenticated user could create and deliver an Entity Analysis dashboard link to a Splunk Enterprise Security user. If the Splunk Enterprise Security user opens the link, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the Splunk Enterprise Security user. The commands could expose or modify some data available to the Splunk Enterprise Security user.
The vulnerability is possible because the Entity Analysis dashboard inserts entity values from a link that an unauthenticated user creates into SPL searches without safely escaping the values.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The unauthenticated user should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Entity analysis dashboard (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/exposure-analytics-and-ueba/entity-analysis-dashboard) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in Updates data. If another user who can access the System Update Status report selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the System Update Status report does not validate destination, signature, and vendor-product values before inserting them into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and System Update Status (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-reports/system-update-status) in the Splunk documentation.

Vulnerability in the Siebel CRM Deployment product of Oracle Siebel CRM (component: Server Infrastructure).  Supported versions that are affected are 17.0-26.9. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Siebel CRM Deployment.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized read access to a subset of Siebel CRM Deployment accessible data and unauthorized ability to cause a partial denial of service (partial DOS) of Siebel CRM Deployment. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 4.8 (Confidentiality and Availability impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:L).

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to edit and run playbooks could modify a child playbook callback handle associated with another playbook run, which could alter the callback behavior of that run.
The vulnerability exists because the Playbook API does not verify that callback-handle updates belong to the related parent and child playbook runs.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to view, edit, and run playbooks and access to at least one container label could retrieve a callback handle from a playbook run outside the container-label scope granted to that account.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not verify that the requested callback handle belongs to the parent playbook run that launched the child playbook.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) and Data access automation API (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/python-playbook-api-reference/8.8.0/automation-api/data-access-automation-api) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to create containers on one label could use the Representational State Transfer (REST) API to create a container with a parent relationship to a container that the user cannot access. This could let the user alter incident lineage across authorization boundaries and identify existing restricted containers.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API accepts a customer-supplied parent relationship when creating a container without authorizing access to the referenced container.
For more information see REST Containers (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/8.6.0/container-endpoints/rest-containers) and Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.8.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to create and view containers for a label could use the Representational State Transfer (REST) API to create a container that references a workbook phase in a case the user cannot view, disclosing the phase name and creating an inconsistent phase association.
The vulnerability exists because the Container REST API does not enforce the same case-scoped authorization when it accepts a workbook-phase reference during container creation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission could cause Splunk SOAR to send the stored root credential for an external credential store to a host that the user controls. Depending on the configuration, the exposed credential could include an access token, application secret, account password, or client certificate.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR reuses the stored credential when the user changes the external credential store endpoint without supplying replacement credentials.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Apps edit permission could cause Splunk SOAR to execute arbitrary code on the host when the user validates an installed app.
The vulnerability is possible because the app validation workflow does not isolate untrusted code from the trusted environment.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with the system_settings permission could change event custom field definitions without the changes appearing in the audit trail, reducing forensic visibility and change accountability.
The issue occurs because Splunk SOAR does not audit custom field definition changes.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to edit artifacts could cause indicator correlation data to retain stale field associations, which can produce incorrect correlation results and event counts.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not remove stale indicator associations when an artifact changes.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to view and edit containers could import a container archive that makes artifacts appear to be part of a case or have notes when no corresponding case associations or notes exist. This could cause Representational State Transfer (REST) API clients and filters to use incorrect artifact state.
The vulnerability is possible because container archive import accepts artifact workflow state from the archive instead of deriving that state from associated cases and notes.
For more information see Splunk SOAR REST API reference (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user who holds a role that can edit and run playbooks in Splunk SOAR could cause Splunk SOAR to run non-read-only actions from a Safe Mode playbook, resulting in unauthorized state changes.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not verify that the playbook run context in an action request matches the context that the server provided.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user who can edit and run playbooks on a container label could associate a custom-function callback with another playbook run. The callback could modify the state of a container outside the authorized scope for that user.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not bind playbook API requests to the trusted playbook run and container context.

In Splunk App for Stream versions below 8.1.7, an unauthenticated user who can reach the Splunk App for Stream Representational State Transfer (REST) API on the management port (8089) could upload an Extensible Markup Language (XML) vocabulary file, which lets the vocabulary upload endpoint read local files accessible to the Splunk process or send outbound requests.
The vulnerability is possible because the vocabulary upload endpoint parses uploaded XML without an application-level policy that blocks external entity resolution.
For more information see About Splunk Stream (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/collect-stream-data/install-and-configure-splunk-stream/8.1/introduction/about-splunk-stream) and restmap.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/9.4/configuration-file-reference/9.4.3-configuration-file-reference/restmap.conf) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk AI Assistant versions below 2.0.0 a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could access data associated with another tenant and cause actions to be attributed to that tenant through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk AI Assistant accepted a client-controlled tenant identifier when selecting the authorization context for a request.

Vulnerability in the Siebel CRM Deployment product of Oracle Siebel CRM (component: Server Infrastructure).  Supported versions that are affected are 17.0-26.9. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows high privileged attacker with logon to the infrastructure where Siebel CRM Deployment executes to compromise Siebel CRM Deployment.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Siebel CRM Deployment accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 4.4 (Confidentiality impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N).

Fabio is an HTTP(S) and TCP router for deploying applications managed by consul. Prior to 1.7.3, route/table.go selects targets using raw req.URL.Path, while proxy/http_proxy.go applies per-route ACL and basic-auth checks to the selected target and forwards the raw path to the origin. Dot-segment, encoded-dot, or repeated-slash variants can fall through to a less restrictive route that reaches the same backend; the backend then normalizes the path and serves the protected resource without the configured access controls. A less restrictive fallback route must reach the same backend; without one, the request returns 404. This issue is fixed in version 1.7.3.

When extra data is allowed (extra=Extra.allow), providing a __pydantic_initialised__ key when validating a Pydantic V1 dataclass makes it considered as already validated, resulting in field values not being validated. The __init__() method of Pydantic V1 dataclasses stores all the provided keyword arguments in the instance __dict__ before validation, so a __pydantic_initialised__ keyword argument overrides the internal flag used to skip validation of already validated instances. As a result, data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into Pydantic V1 dataclasses allowing extra data. The issue was fixed in Pydantic 1.10.27. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Vulnerability in the Siebel CRM Deployment product of Oracle Siebel CRM (component: Server Infrastructure).  Supported versions that are affected are 17.0-26.9. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows high privileged attacker with logon to the infrastructure where Siebel CRM Deployment executes to compromise Siebel CRM Deployment.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized read access to a subset of Siebel CRM Deployment accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 1.9 (Confidentiality impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N).

Vulnerability in the Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition product of Oracle Java SE (component: Compiler).  Supported versions that are affected are Oracle Java SE: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3; Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.21.0.3 and  21.0.13.0.3; Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service. Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Reconciliation Manage).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Use of uninitialized memory when processing certain font files in X.Org libXfont before 2.0.10 could be used by authenticated attackers to crash the X server.

Connaisseur is an admission controller that integrates container image signature verification into a Kubernetes cluster. Prior to 3.11.1, the Cosign validator counts valid signature layers rather than distinct trust roots for trustRoot: "*" policies using an explicit threshold or an implicit require-all policy. An attacker who controls one configured trust root's signing key and can attach multiple signatures to an image can satisfy a threshold intended to require multiple independent roots, causing admission without the intended signer quorum. Policies using a single trust root or the required option are not affected. This issue is fixed in 3.11.1.

This issue allows an attacker to inspect restricted course material and copy it into their own wiki pages, leading to unauthorized information disclosure.

CKAN is an open-source data management system for data hubs and data portals. Prior to 2.10.11 and 2.11.6, the web user registration flow authenticates a newly registered account without first regenerating the session identifier when server-side session storage is configured. An attacker who can set a session cookie in a victim's browser or obtain the victim's current valid session identifier can reuse that identifier after the victim registers, gaining access to the new account. CKAN uses cookie-based sessions by default, and web registration is disabled by default through ckan.auth.create_user_via_web. This issue is fixed in CKAN 2.10.11, 2.11.6, and 2.12.0.

ALTCHA is a Go library for creating and verifying ALTCHA challenges. Prior to 2.1.0, parseServerSignature can leave ServerSignatureVerificationData.Extra uninitialized when url.ParseQuery returns partial values and an error for a malformed percent escape in VerificationData. A later write of an unknown parsed key to the nil map panics before VerifyServerSignature or VerifyServerSignatureSafe completes signature verification, so an unauthenticated client can abort a request. Standard net/http recovers the request goroutine, while application goroutines or frameworks without recovery can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 2.1.0.

In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.8.15 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the policy enforcers do not let a revoke win over a grant in two kinds of permission checks. Checks of several permissions at once compare the highest grant weight with the highest revoke weight across all requested permissions instead of per permission, so the "check permissions" API (`POST /api/2/checkPermissions`, available since 3.7.0) can report a set of permissions as granted although one of them is revoked. Partial permission checks, which authorize retrieving Things and Policies and determine the receivers of events, count a grant on a sub-resource although the same permission is revoked on that sub-resource for another subject of the same authorization context (or, with the memory-optimized policy evaluator, for the same subject). A requester can thereby learn about the existence of Things and Policies and receive metadata without any readable content, and an application relying on the check permissions result may grant access the policy denies. The content of retrieved Things and Policies is still filtered correctly, and modifications are not affected.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the resolved policy view (`GET /api/2/policies/{policyId}?policy-view=resolved`) does not restrict merged policy content to what the caller may read in the policy it originates from. Imported and namespace-root entries are returned in full as soon as the caller may read any part of them in the source policy, entries of transitive imports and of the imports of namespace-root policies are only checked against the intermediate policy, and content copied into an entry by `references`, also from another entry of the same policy, is not checked against the referenced entry. An authenticated caller with READ on a policy can therefore read subjects, resources and granted/revoked permissions of policy entries that are hidden from them, including by explicit revokes, when reading the originating policy directly.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 1.1.0 to 3.9.8, when pre-authentication is enabled, the gateway service accepts the pre-authenticated subject not only from the `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` HTTP header set by a trusted reverse proxy, but also from an undocumented `x-ditto-pre-authenticated` URL query parameter that a client can set. A reverse proxy that only overwrites the header therefore does not stop clients from supplying their own subject. With the default configuration of the Ditto Helm chart (`global.jwtOnly: false`, which implicitly enables pre-authentication), the bundled nginx skips HTTP Basic authentication for any request with an `Authorization: Bearer` header and forwards it without the pre-authentication header. An unauthenticated remote attacker can send an invalid Bearer token together with the query parameter to authenticate as any chosen policy subject. Pre-authentication succeeds before the JWT is validated, so the attacker can read and modify Things and Policies with that subject's permissions. As a mitigation, disable pre-authentication in the gateway (`ENABLE_PRE_AUTHENTICATION=false`) or, when using the Helm chart, configure `global.jwtOnly: true`.

Go-Guerrilla SMTP Daemon is a lightweight SMTP server written in Go. In 1.6.7 and earlier, according to the repository advisory's structured affected range, server.go defines the seven-byte cmdXCLIENT token, but the XCLIENT handler slices input[8:] after matching only that seven-byte verb, so a bare command causes an out-of-bounds panic in handleClient and terminates the daemon because that connection goroutine does not recover the panic. The issue is reachable by an unauthenticated client when the non-default xclient_on setting is enabled; no HELO command is required. The repository fix is present in version 1.6.7-1.

MISP contains a vulnerability in the cryptographic signature verification of protected events. When a MISP instance signs a protected event for synchronization, it strips all whitespace from the JSON body before computing the PGP signature (preg_replace("/\s+/", "", $data)). The receiving instance performs the same whitespace-stripping before verification. Because the signature covers only the whitespace-free representation, a network relay positioned between two MISP instances can insert whitespace characters into JSON object keys (effectively renaming fields) or into identifier values such as UUIDs, timestamps, and distribution fields without invalidating the signature. The receiving instance accepts the modified event as authentic.

The vulnerability affects the protected event synchronization path: event creation (EventsController::add), event editing (EventsController::edit), event viewing (EventsController::view1), and server-to-server pull synchronization (ServerSyncTool, Server model). An attacker with a network position to intercept and modify traffic between MISP instances can alter the semantic content of protected events while the PGP signature still validates, undermining the integrity guarantees that protected events are designed to provide.

The fix introduces two complementary mechanisms. First, a post-verification scan rejects any received body that contains whitespace in JSON keys (except under Galaxy cluster 'meta' keys) or in identifier-like values (uuid, id, timestamp, distribution, date). Second, a new exact-byte signature scheme (x-pgp-signature-v2) signs the body as transmitted, without whitespace normalization. MISP 3.0 and later peers exchange this exact-byte signature; older peers retain the legacy whitespace-stripped signature. A signature_version field is embedded in protected events so that a 3.0 receiver refuses a body carrying that marker if only the legacy signature is present. Both mechanisms together close the whitespace-injection vector while preserving backward compatibility with pre-3.0 instances.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.4.0 to 3.9.8, Thing fields a requester is not allowed to read can be disclosed through the `condition` and `live-channel-condition` headers, which are evaluated against the

  full Thing: the READ check of `live-channel-condition` is skipped when a `condition` header is also present on Thing query commands (3.0.0 to 3.9.8); both headers are evaluated without any authorization
  on WoT Thing Description requests (`Accept: application/td+json`) when WoT TD permission filtering is not active (by default in 3.0.0 to 3.8.14, in 2.4.x with WoT integration enabled, and in 3.9.x with
  filtering disabled); the `condition` of live messages and live events is evaluated without a READ check, and of claim messages without any permission (3.1.0 to 3.9.8); and the twin response of a Thing
  query with a non-matching `live-channel-condition` is returned without filtering it by the policy (3.0.0 to 3.9.8). This allows an authenticated user to read Thing fields they are not allowed to read, in
  some cases without any permission on the Thing.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Installation and Configuration).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized update, insert or delete access to some of Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology accessible data as well as  unauthorized read access to a subset of Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 4.8 (Confidentiality and Integrity impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N).

MISP contains an authorization and input-validation flaw in its event push mechanism. When a user with push permissions initiates a push of events to a remote MISP instance, the system fails to enforce two critical checks: (1) it does not verify that an event is published before including it in the push, allowing unpublished (i.e., not yet publicly shared) events to be transmitted to the remote server; and (2) it does not verify that the pushing user has read access to the event, causing events the user cannot fetch to be sent as empty event shells, thereby disclosing the existence and metadata of events the user is not authorized to view. Additionally, the remote server's reply selecting which offered events to accept is used without validating that the selected identifiers actually correspond to events in the offered set, potentially allowing the remote to reference events outside the intended scope. The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with push permissions on the source MISP instance and a configured push target. The security impact is unauthorized disclosure of confidential threat-intelligence data (unpublished events and events restricted by user permissions) to a remote MISP instance that should not receive them.

Authorization bypass through a user-controlled key in the PuppetDB facts terminus used by Puppet Server allows a client holding any valid agent certificate to overwrite the facts, including trusted facts, that PuppetDB stores for a different node. In Puppet Enterprise deployments where task permissions are scoped to node groups defined by facts or trusted facts, this can allow a user to run tasks on nodes outside their permitted scope.

The failed-login limiter of the JTL-Wawi
synchronisation interface of JTL-Shop derives the client identity from the
client-controlled X-Forwarded-For header and counts requests without credentials as failed
logins. An unauthenticated remote attacker can block the synchronisation
between JTL-Shop and JTL-Wawi with a few requests and repeat this
indefinitely, so that orders are no longer handed over to JTL-Wawi. No data is disclosed
and no code is executed.

Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows low privileged attacker with logon to the infrastructure where Oracle Hyperion Planning executes to compromise Oracle Hyperion Planning.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized update, insert or delete access to some of Oracle Hyperion Planning accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 2.5 (Integrity impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N).

The web installer of JTL-Shop executes its
state-changing installation tasks without checking whether the shop is already
installed, and was not removed or locked after the installation. An unauthenticated
remote attacker who can reach the installer directory can supply their own
database credentials, create administrator and synchronisation accounts and
overwrite the shop configuration. This can lead to a full takeover of
the shop, including code execution on the server.

A flaw was found in nbdkit. The qcow2dec filter's zstd_compressed_cluster() function incorrectly sets the ZSTD input buffer size to the uncompressed cluster size instead of the compressed buffer size. A crafted QCOW2 image with ZSTD-compressed clusters can trigger a heap over-read, leading to a denial of service and potentially exposing heap memory.

Insufficient Session Expiration vulnerability in the Apache Iggy server HTTP transport. A self-issued JSON Web Token (JWT) identified the user only by numeric user ID, and a new user takes the lowest free ID. After an administrator deleted a user, that user's unexpired token, or a token refreshed from it while the ID was free, authenticated as the next account created with that ID and had that account's permissions. Only deployments with HTTP enabled are affected.

This issue affects Apache Iggy: through 0.9.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.10.0, which fixes the issue.

Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with access to the physical communication segment attached to the hardware where the Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management executes to compromise Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized creation, deletion or modification access to critical data or all Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management accessible data as well as  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 6.8 (Confidentiality and Integrity impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N).

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the Apache Iggy server. The system snapshot command (GetSnapshot on the binary transports and POST /snapshot on HTTP) checked only that the caller was logged in, not the read_servers or manage_servers permission. Any authenticated user, including a user with no permissions, could download a diagnostic archive with the server log files, the host process list, a file system listing and the runtime server configuration. The runtime configuration contains the HTTP JWT signing secret and the message encryption key when they are set in the configuration. If HTTP is enabled, the user could use the signing secret to create tokens for any account, including root.

This issue affects Apache Iggy: before 0.9.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.10.0, which fixes the issue.

Vulnerability in the MySQL Cluster product of Oracle MySQL (component: Cluster: JS module).  Supported versions that are affected are 8.0.0-8.0.50, 8.4.0-8.4.13, 9.7.0-9.7.4 and  26.10. Poweradmin is a web-based DNS administration tool for PowerDNS server. From 4.0.0 until 4.2.6, 4.3.5, and 4.4.1, lib/Domain/Service/MfaService.php verifies email second-factor codes through MfaService::verifyCode() without limiting failed attempts, and lib/Application/Controller/MfaVerifyController.php logs failures without throttling them. An attacker who knows the user's password can repeatedly guess the six-digit code during its ten-minute validity period when email MFA is enabled, potentially bypassing the second factor; the advisory notes MFA is disabled by default and that the practical request rate was not measured. This issue is fixed in versions 4.2.6, 4.3.5, and 4.4.1.

In Eclipse versions 1.5-1.6.13, 2.0.0-2.0.22 and 2.1.0-2.1.2, the client library libmosquitto does not reject Will messages with payloads greater than 65535 bytes when calling `mosquitto_will_set()` or `mosquitto_will_set_v5()`. This results in up to 65535 bytes of uninitialised heap memory being transmitted as the Will.



This can be mitigated by only passing payloads with a maximum length of 65535 bytes.

ServiceNow has remediated an information disclosure vulnerability that was identified in the ServiceNow AI Platform. This vulnerability could cause a user's plaintext password to be persisted in a system table, potentially exposing that password to a user who otherwise would not be entitled to view it.





ServiceNow remediated the vulnerability through security updates that address the unintended persistence of plaintext credentials. We are not currently aware of malicious exploitation against ServiceNow instances. We recommend customers promptly apply appropriate updates or upgrade to a patched release if they have not already done so.

In the Apache Airflow Microsoft Azure provider 10.2.0 through 15.3.0, `S3ToAzureBlobStorageOperator` turned off TLS certificate verification for its connection to Amazon S3 by default (`s3_verify=False`), whatever the AWS connection's own verification settings were. An attacker positioned on the network between an Airflow worker and S3 could intercept that traffic, read the signed requests and alter the listed object keys and the copied file contents. Deployments are affected when a Dag uses `S3ToAzureBlobStorageOperator` without setting `s3_verify`. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-microsoft-azure 15.3.1 or later, which uses the AWS connection's verification settings by default.
